title: Fitting copper pipe clips and running a pipe through a joist
subtitle: Space and fix pipe clips on a wall run, drill a notch or hole through a timber joist, and route copper pipe cleanly to the next fitting
excerpt: How to fit pipe clips to a masonry or timber surface and route a copper pipe through a timber floor joist. Covers clip spacing, drilling notches or holes, filling notches with a nail plate, and clipping the run.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK Water Regulations Advisory Scheme guidance on pipe installation (open access). Building Regulations Approved Document A on notching and drilling joists.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plastic or chrome metal saddle clip that holds a copper pipe against a wall or joist face. Available for 15 mm and 22 mm copper. Screwed to the surface with a single wood or masonry screw. The clip holds the pipe firmly but not so tightly that it prevents thermal expansion along the run.

Building Regulations Approved Document A limits where timber joists can be notched or drilled for pipes and cables. Notches must be in the top third of the joist depth, within the zone one-tenth to one-quarter of the clear span from the support. Holes may be drilled in the neutral zone (centre quarter of the joist depth) at any point along the span but no closer than 3 diameters between holes. Oversized notches weaken the joist structurally.

Clip spacing on a wall run

For 15 mm copper pipe on a horizontal run, space clips at no more than 1.2 m centres. On a vertical run, space at 1.8 m centres. For 22 mm pipe, 1.8 m horizontal and 2.4 m vertical. At every bend or change of direction, fit a clip within 150 mm on each side of the bend. Clips on a masonry wall use a 6 mm masonry plug and screw; clips into timber use a 30 mm No. 8 wood screw.

A notch in the top of a joist allows a pipe to pass through below the floor surface. The notch must be in the top third of the joist depth, within the zone that is one-tenth to one-quarter of the span from the wall. For a typical 150 mm deep joist, the notch is cut in the top 50 mm. Cut the notch width at 15 mm or 22 mm (matching the pipe) with a jigsaw or chisel. Do not notch deeper than 12.5 mm (one-twelfth of the joist depth for a standard joist). Fit a steel nail plate over the notch to prevent a flooring nail penetrating the pipe.

For a concealed run, a hole drilled through the neutral zone (the central quarter of the joist depth) is structurally acceptable at any point along the span. The hole diameter must not exceed one-quarter of the joist depth; for a 150 mm joist that is 37 mm. Space holes at least three hole-diameters apart (a 20 mm hole: minimum 60 mm between hole centres). Drill with a long auger bit or a flat spade bit; keep the bit centred on the joist height.

attrs.symptom: Pipe makes a clicking or ticking noise when hot water runs through it
attrs.cause: Thermal expansion is causing the pipe to rub against clips or joist edges.
attrs.fix: Check that clips are not overtightened. Where the pipe passes through a hole in a joist, wrap the pipe in a short sleeve of foam pipe lagging to prevent direct metal-on-timber contact.

attrs.symptom: The joist develops a slight flex or bounce after the notch
attrs.cause: The notch was cut too deep or in the wrong zone of the joist.
attrs.fix: Fit a sister joist alongside the notched joist, fixed at each end to the wall plates. Consult a structural engineer if the bounce is pronounced.
